Today: The hottest day of the week will be this afternoon with highs 
into the mid to upper 90s regionwide. The hottest temperatures will 
be felt in the Lewiston-Clarkston Valley where temperatures are 
expected to top out between 100-103 degrees. A heat advisory is in 
effect starting at noon today and will continue through Wednesday. 
The hot and dry conditions won't do anything to curb fire activity 
with the active fires in the Cascades. The Little Giant Fire and 
Sinlahekin Fire were active on Monday, and the hotter, drier weather 
will only increase the potential for more activity today. Expect 
increased smoke production, but winds aloft from the east will 
generally transport this smoke into western Washington.

Tonight through Thursday night: A trough of lower pressure will dig 
across the eastern Pacific and displace the ridge of high pressure 
eastward over this period. The displacement will be more 
gradual on Wednesday and this will result in a push of marine 
air through the Cascade gaps. The result of this will be 
increased westerly winds through the Kititas Valley, the 
Wenatchee River Valley, and out over the far western Columbia 
Basin. The marine layer looks to remain below 4,000 ft MSL 
through at least mid afternoon on Wednesday. It does deepen more
so heading into the evening hours up to around 5,000 ft AGL. 
That will be fairly late in the day for much if any of that 
cooler marine air to spill through with much impact on high 
temperatures. Thus, Wednesday looks to be another hot, dry day,
but also with winds a bit breezier near the Cascades. This 
combination will result in an elevated fire weather situation.

The potential for convection carries a good amount of uncertainty. 
The latest convective allowing models are hinting at a better 
potential for convection developing over the Northeast Blue 
Mountains that drifts off to the northeast toward Lewiston and 
Pullman/Moscow for this evening. Forcing aloft is rather weak and 
the question will be if convection will be able to punch through a 
considerable amount of CIN in place of around 50 J/kg. That may be 
too much negative energy to overcome for air parcels to reach their 
Level of Free Convection late this afternoon into this evening. 
There is a better chance over the mountains of northeast
Washington and over the Idaho Panhandle on Wednesday. The 
trough will be in closer proximity with a weak shortwave 
disturbance supplying at least weak synoptic sale lift. The 
timing of the wave looks to be in the afternoon with around 
500-1000 J/kg of surface based CAPE, but there will also be 
50-80 J/kg of CIN as well. Thunderstorm coverage is expected to
be isolated without good alignment of instability with forcing.
Any convection that is able to break through the cap will be 
capable of developing quickly. Inverted-V sounding profiles 
would support strong outflow winds, and potentially microbursts.

A cold front sweeps across on Thursday and this will tighten up the 
pressure gradient with gusty westerly winds by the afternoon. 
Sustained winds of 15-25 mph with gusts of up to 30-40 mph is 
expected. Temperatures will be 9-12 degrees cooler, but still dry 
and the combination of stronger winds with minimum relative 
humidity down to between 20-25% will be enough for elevated to 
locally critical fire weather conditions. Convection on Thursday
is expected occur primarily north and east of the region in BC 
and Montana respectively.

Friday through Tuesday: The far extended portion of the forecast
will feature cooler temperatures closer to seasonal normals. 
Not much moisture to speak of, but a disturbance swinging 
through will bring a 15-30% chance for showers mainly over the 
mountains. There will also be a 20% chance for thunderstorms 
near the Canadian border for Saturday afternoon. Winds will be 
breezy at times, but the cooler temperatures looks to keep 
relative humidity levels above critical thresholds. /SVH
